read.plain:
Burn depth is how far through the skin the injury goes, and it is the single most useful thing you can describe about a burn.

Superficial burns involve only the outermost layer. Red, dry, painful, and no blisters. Sunburn is the familiar example. They heal on their own without scarring.

Partial thickness burns go through that outer layer into the dermis beneath. These are the ones with blisters. The surface is moist and weeping, mottled red or pink, and they are intensely painful — more painful than deeper burns, because the nerve endings are damaged and exposed but still working.

Full thickness burns destroy every layer of skin. They look white, waxy, leathery or charred, and the surface is dry rather than weeping. And they are typically painless in the burned area, because the nerve endings have been destroyed along with everything else.

That last point is the one that matters most, because it inverts the intuition everybody has. The worst burns hurt the least. A patient calmly telling you a white leathery patch on their arm does not hurt is describing something far more serious than the person screaming about a blistered hand.

Do not grade a burn by how much it hurts.

There is a subtlety here. A full thickness burn is almost always ringed by partial thickness burn at its edges, where the heat was less intense. So the patient usually is in pain — from the border rather than the centre. If you press the middle of a full thickness area and they feel nothing, that is your finding.

Burns are usually mixed. One injury commonly contains superficial, partial and full thickness areas, and judging which is which early is genuinely difficult even for people who do it often. Burns also evolve — an area that looks partial thickness today can declare itself as full thickness over the following days. So describe what you see rather than committing to a confident classification, and say it is difficult to judge if it is.

When extent is calculated for fluid decisions, superficial burns are not counted. Only partial and full thickness areas go into the number. Counting the sunburn on somebody's shoulders inflates the figure and can lead to over-treatment.

One final thing to look for. A full thickness burn that goes all the way around a limb, or around the chest, is a problem beyond the burn itself. Burned skin is leathery and does not stretch, and the tissue underneath swells. Around an arm, that acts like a tourniquet and cuts off the circulation. Around a chest, it can restrict breathing. If you find a circumferential full thickness burn, check circulation below it, watch the breathing, and say so clearly at handover — it is a surgical problem with a short fuse.
read.standard: Burn depth denotes the extent of dermal penetration and determines healing, scarring and surgical requirement. Superficial burns involve the epidermis alone, presenting as erythematous, dry and painful without blistering, and heal without scarring. Partial thickness burns extend into the dermis, producing blistering, moist mottled erythematous surfaces and severe pain owing to exposed but viable nerve endings. Full thickness burns destroy all dermal layers, appearing white, waxy, leathery or charred with a dry surface, and are characteristically insensate owing to nerve ending destruction. Severity therefore correlates inversely with pain within the burned area. Full thickness burns are typically bounded by partial thickness injury, preserving peripheral sensation. Burns are commonly of mixed depth, with early classification unreliable and depth frequently evolving over subsequent days. Superficial burns are excluded from body surface area calculation; only partial and full thickness areas are counted. Circumferential full thickness burns produce constriction as underlying oedema develops within inelastic eschar, compromising distal perfusion in extremities and ventilation in the thorax.

eli_new.analogy: The worst burns hurt least, because the nerves that would have reported the pain were destroyed by the thing that caused it.
eli_new.body: Two errors. Grading severity by pain, which gets it exactly backwards. And counting superficial burns in the extent, which inflates the number and can lead to a patient being over-treated for a burn that was partly sunburn.

story.title: It doesn't hurt
story.dispatch: Medic 3 — kitchen burn, 44-year-old male, forearm.
story.body:
He was more embarrassed than distressed and kept saying it was not that bad because it barely hurt at all.

The centre of it was white and leathery and he felt nothing when it was touched. The ring of blistered skin around the outside was where all his pain was coming from.

The part that did not hurt was the part that needed a surgeon.

concepts.title: Rule of nines and the palm method
key_points: Burn extent is expressed as a percentage of total body surface area, and it drives fluid decisions and destination
The rule of nines divides the adult body into areas of nine percent or multiples of nine
Adult: head and neck 9, each arm 9, each leg 18, front of trunk 18, back of trunk 18, genitalia 1
The paediatric proportions differ because a child's head is proportionally much larger and the legs proportionally smaller
Infant: head 18, each arm 9, each leg 14, front of trunk 18, back of trunk 18
The intermediate ages between infant and adult are not covered by a simple rule, and a Lund-Browder chart is used for them at hospital
The palm method estimates scattered or irregular burns: the patient's own palm is approximately one percent of their body surface
Use the patient's palm, not yours — the estimate is relative to their body
Superficial burns are excluded from the total, and field estimates are approximations rather than measurements

Using your own palm rather than the patient's
Including superficial burns in the total
Presenting a field estimate as a precise figure

read.plain:
Burn extent is expressed as a percentage of the body surface, and it matters because it drives fluid resuscitation decisions at hospital and helps decide whether the patient goes to a burns centre.

The rule of nines divides the adult body into regions that are nine percent or multiples of it. For an adult: head and neck nine. Each arm nine. Each leg eighteen. The front of the trunk eighteen. The back of the trunk eighteen. And the genitalia one, which is what makes the total come to a hundred.

Worth noticing that a leg is a fifth of the body and an arm is a tenth of it — people consistently underestimate legs.

Children are not small adults, and the proportions genuinely differ. A child's head is a much larger share of their body and their legs are a smaller share. For an infant: head eighteen, each arm nine, each leg fourteen, front of trunk eighteen, back of trunk eighteen.

So a burn to the head that is nine percent in an adult is eighteen percent in an infant — double. Using adult figures on a small child substantially underestimates a head burn and overestimates a leg burn.

Now the honest part. Between infant and adult there is no clean rule, because the proportions shift gradually with age. Hospitals use a Lund-Browder chart, which has age-adjusted values for each region. I am not giving you an intermediate table here, because those values vary between sources and a confidently wrong figure for a seven-year-old is worse than saying you estimated it. If you have a child between those two extremes, estimate with the palm method, describe what is burned in plain terms — 'the whole of the front of the chest and all of the right arm' — and let the receiving team apply the chart.

The palm method handles scattered and irregular burns, which the rule of nines does badly. The patient's own palm is approximately one percent of their body surface. Splashes, spatter, patchy burns — count palms.

Two details. Use the patient's palm, not yours: the estimate is relative to their body, and your hand on a child's chest gives a wildly wrong answer. And sources differ on whether the one percent includes the fingers or the palm alone, so check which your text uses.

Finally: superficial burns are excluded, and everything here is an estimate. Field burn percentages are routinely revised at hospital, and that is expected. Give your figure, say how you arrived at it, and describe what you actually saw — the description survives your arithmetic being adjusted.
read.standard: Burn extent is quantified as percentage total body surface area, informing fluid resuscitation and destination decisions. The rule of nines apportions the adult body in increments of nine percent: head and neck nine, each upper limb nine, each lower limb eighteen, anterior trunk eighteen, posterior trunk eighteen, and genitalia one, totalling one hundred. Paediatric proportions differ owing to relatively greater cephalic and lesser lower limb surface area. Infant values are: head eighteen, each upper limb nine, each lower limb fourteen, anterior trunk eighteen, posterior trunk eighteen. Intermediate ages are not accommodated by a simple rule and are assessed at hospital using an age-adjusted Lund-Browder chart. The palm method estimates irregular or scattered burns, the patient's own palmar surface approximating one percent of their total body surface area; the patient's palm rather than the provider's is used, and sources differ regarding inclusion of the digits. Superficial burns are excluded from calculation, and prehospital estimates constitute approximations subject to revision.

concepts.title: Thermal, chemical, electrical and radiation burns
key_points: Stop the burning process first, whatever the cause — that is the common first step
Thermal: remove from the source, cool with room temperature water briefly, then cover and keep the patient warm
Cooling too long or with anything cold causes hypothermia, particularly in children and large burns
Chemical: brush off dry powder first, then irrigate with copious running water for a prolonged period per protocol
Do not attempt to neutralise a chemical — the reaction generates heat and makes the injury worse
Electrical: the visible wounds are entry and exit points and the damage runs between them, so the injury is far bigger than it looks
Electrical injury can cause cardiac arrest and rhythm disturbances, and can fracture bones through violent muscle contraction
Never touch an electrical patient until the source is confirmed isolated by someone qualified to say so
Radiation: time, distance and shielding; do not enter and do not become a casualty
misconceptions: Cooling a large burn for too long and causing hypothermia
Trying to neutralise an acid or alkali
Judging an electrical burn by the size of the visible wounds
Approaching an electrical patient before isolation is confirmed
Irrigating a dry powder chemical before brushing it off
exam_favorites: Electrical damage runs between entry and exit

read.plain:
Whatever the cause, the first step is the same: stop the burning process. Everything else follows from that.

Thermal burns. Get the patient away from the source, and remove burning or smouldering clothing and anything hot that is still against the skin — but leave anything stuck to the burn where it is. Cool the burned area with room temperature water, briefly.

That word briefly matters. Cooling relieves pain and limits ongoing damage, and beyond a short period it stops helping and starts causing hypothermia. A patient with a large burn has lost the skin that normally keeps heat in, and pouring water on them cools the whole body, not just the burn. Children are especially vulnerable because of their surface-to-volume ratio. So: cool the burn, then stop, dry them, cover them and keep them warm. Cooling and warming in sequence sounds contradictory and it is exactly right. Follow your protocol for the duration.

Chemical burns. The order here catches people out. If the chemical is a dry powder, brush it off first. Adding water to certain dry chemicals activates them, and irrigating before brushing washes activated chemical across more skin. Brush it off, then irrigate.

Then irrigate with copious running water for a prolonged period — far longer than feels necessary, and the duration is in your protocol. Remove contaminated clothing and jewellery while irrigating, because the chemical is in the fabric and keeps working.

And do not try to neutralise anything. Not acid with alkali, not alkali with acid. The reaction itself generates heat, so you add a thermal burn on top of the chemical one, in tissue that is already injured. Water, and lots of it.

Electrical burns are the most deceptive injury in this module. You will see an entry wound and an exit wound, often small, often on a hand and a foot. Between them, the current travelled through the body, and everything on that path — muscle, nerve, vessel, heart — took the energy. The visible burns are the two ends of an injury you cannot see any of.

So expect the injury to be far bigger than it looks. Expect cardiac effects: electricity causes arrest and rhythm disturbances, and a patient who was shocked and now seems fine still needs monitoring. Expect fractures and dislocations, because current causes violent muscle contraction, and people break bones and dislocate shoulders through their own muscle power. And expect the muscle damage to behave like a crush injury.

Safety is absolute here. Do not touch the patient, and do not touch anything the patient is touching, until the power is confirmed isolated by somebody qualified to confirm it. Not somebody saying they think it is off. Confirmed, by the utility company or a competent person. Downed power lines can energise ground, fences and vehicles for a considerable distance. Every year rescuers die at these scenes doing something that felt obviously necessary.

Radiation. Three principles: minimise time, maximise distance, use shielding. This is a specialist scene. Do not enter, do not improvise, and stay well back until the people with the equipment and the training arrive. A rescuer who becomes a casualty has helped nobody.
read.standard: Cessation of the burning process constitutes the initial intervention across all burn mechanisms. Thermal burns require removal from source, removal of burning or smouldering clothing and retained hot material while leaving adherent material in situ, and brief cooling with room temperature water; prolonged cooling produces hypothermia, particularly in paediatric patients and extensive burns where integumentary thermoregulation is lost, and is followed by drying, covering and active warming. Chemical burns require removal of dry particulate by brushing prior to irrigation, as premature irrigation activates and disperses certain agents, followed by prolonged copious irrigation with running water and removal of contaminated clothing and jewellery. Neutralisation is contraindicated, as the reaction is exothermic and superimposes thermal injury. Electrical injury produces entry and exit wounds with extensive intervening tissue damage along the current path; associated findings include cardiac arrest and dysrhythmia, fractures and dislocations from tetanic muscle contraction, and rhabdomyolysis. Scene approach is contraindicated until isolation is confirmed by a competent authority, as energised ground, fencing and vehicles extend the hazard. Radiation incidents are managed by minimising time, maximising distance and employing shielding, with entry restricted to appropriately equipped specialist responders.

eli_new.analogy: An electrical burn is a tunnel with two small doors. You can see both doors and none of the tunnel, and all the damage is in the tunnel.
eli_new.body: Two things that feel wrong and are right. Cool the burn and then deliberately warm the patient — those are not contradictory, they are sequential. And brush dry chemical off before you reach for water, because water on some dry chemicals makes them worse.

He felt fine, wanted to go back to work, and could not understand the fuss over two small marks.

The current had gone in at one and out at the other, and everything on the line between them had been in its path.

concepts.title: Airway burns and inhalation injury
key_points: Inhalation injury kills more burn patients than the skin burns do, and it can be present with almost no external burn
The warning signs are the story and the face: an enclosed-space fire, soot around the mouth or nose, singed facial or nasal hair, burns to the face or neck
Hoarseness, a change in voice, stridor, a brassy cough, carbon in the sputum and difficulty swallowing are the airway declaring itself
Swelling develops over minutes to hours, so an airway that is patent now may not be later — this is why these patients go early
An airway that is beginning to swell will only get more difficult, so early transport and early notification are the treatment
Give high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather, and remember that a normal oximeter reading means nothing after a fire
Assume carbon monoxide in any enclosed-space fire, and consider cyanide from burning synthetic materials
Sit the patient up if they tolerate it, keep them calm, and handle the airway as little as possible
Do not be reassured by a comfortable patient: the dangerous phase is the one that has not started yet
misconceptions: Being reassured by a patient who is talking normally now
Trusting a pulse oximeter after a fire
Waiting to see whether the airway deteriorates before transporting
Repeatedly instrumenting an irritable airway
exam_favorites: Warning signs on the face and in the story
The oximeter lies after a fire

read.plain:
Inhalation injury is the thing that kills burn patients. More than the burns themselves, and often in patients whose skin damage is unimpressive. So this concept is about recognising a threat that has not arrived yet.

The warning comes from two places: the story, and the face.

The story. Was this a fire in an enclosed space? A house, a vehicle, a basement, a container? Enclosed-space fires fill the space with hot gases and products of combustion and give the patient nowhere to go. Was the patient unconscious at any point, or trapped, or found in the room rather than outside it? Those details matter more than the burns.

The face. Soot around the mouth or in the nostrils. Singed facial hair, eyebrows, or hairs inside the nose. Burns to the face or neck. Any of those means hot gas passed across that face and into the airway behind it.

Then listen. Hoarseness or any change of voice. Stridor. A hard brassy cough. Black-flecked sputum. Difficulty or pain on swallowing, or drooling. Those are not warning signs of a future problem; they are the airway telling you it is already swelling.

Here is what makes this dangerous, and it is the whole reason the concept exists. The swelling develops over minutes to hours. A patient who is talking normally, comfortably, with a clear voice may be perfectly patent right now and progressively obstructing over the next hour. The comfortable patient in front of you is not the patient who will arrive.

Which means the treatment is time. Get them moving early, and tell the hospital early — because an airway that is starting to swell only becomes more difficult to manage as the hour goes on, and the people who can secure it want to do so before it becomes impossible. Notification is genuinely one of the most valuable things you can do here.

Give high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather. And remember the pulse oximeter problem from carbon monoxide: after a fire, a saturation of 99 percent tells you nothing, because the machine cannot distinguish carbon monoxide from oxygen. Do not let a comfortable number contribute to a decision to slow down.

Assume carbon monoxide in any enclosed-space fire. Consider cyanide as well, because burning synthetic materials — furniture, foam, carpet, plastics — release it, and fire victims frequently have both.

Practically: sit them up if they tolerate it, keep them calm, and interfere with the airway as little as you can. An irritable, swelling airway that is repeatedly instrumented can spasm shut. Watch it, support it, oxygenate it, and go.
read.standard: Inhalation injury constitutes the leading cause of mortality in burn patients and may occur with minimal cutaneous burn. Historical indicators include enclosed-space fire, loss of consciousness, entrapment and discovery within the fire compartment. Examination findings include perioral and nasal soot, singed facial, nasal and eyebrow hair, and facial or cervical burns. Symptoms indicating established airway involvement comprise hoarseness or voice change, stridor, brassy cough, carbonaceous sputum, odynophagia and drooling. Oedema progresses over minutes to hours, so current patency does not predict continued patency; early transport and prearrival notification constitute the principal interventions, as airway management difficulty increases progressively. High-concentration oxygen is administered by non-rebreather mask. Pulse oximetry is unreliable following fire exposure owing to carboxyhaemoglobin. Carbon monoxide toxicity is presumed in enclosed-space fires, with cyanide toxicity considered where synthetic materials have combusted. Patients are positioned upright as tolerated, kept calm, and airway instrumentation minimised to avoid precipitating laryngospasm.

eli_new.analogy: A swelling airway is a door closing slowly. The question is never whether it is open now. It is how open it will be in forty minutes, and whether you will be somewhere useful by then.
eli_new.body: The trap is a comfortable patient. Someone who walked out of a house fire, is talking normally and has a clear voice can obstruct over the next hour. Nothing about how they look right now tells you about the hour ahead — the story and the face do.

He was entirely comfortable, and that told nobody anything at all about the next forty minutes.

concepts.title: Burn management and transport criteria
key_points: Stop the burning, remove jewellery and constricting items early before swelling makes it impossible, and leave anything stuck to the burn
Cover burns with a dry sterile dressing; do not use ointments, creams, butter, ice or anything else
Do not break blisters — intact skin is a barrier against infection
Burn patients lose heat rapidly because the skin that retains it is damaged, so keeping them warm is a priority
Assess and treat other injuries: a burn is visually dominant and distracts from fractures, bleeding and head injury
Burns to the face, hands, feet, genitalia or across a joint, and circumferential burns, are significant regardless of size
Burns in the very young and the very old are more serious at the same extent
Specific burn centre criteria are set locally and by regional burn services — use yours
Consider non-accidental injury where the pattern does not match the history, particularly in children and vulnerable adults
misconceptions: Applying creams or ointments to a burn
Breaking blisters
Leaving rings on a burned hand
Being so absorbed by the burn that other injuries are missed
Letting a burn patient get cold
exam_favorites: Nothing on the burn but a dry dressing
Special areas matter regardless of size

read.plain:
Once the burning has stopped, burn care is mostly about a short list of things to do and a longer list of things not to.

Do remove rings, watches, bracelets and anything constricting, and do it early. Burned tissue swells, and swelling around a ring turns it into a tourniquet on a finger. Ten minutes later it may not come off at all. This is a small action with a large consequence and it gets forgotten in the drama.

Do leave anything that is stuck to the burn where it is. Melted fabric fused to skin comes away with the skin. Cut around it and leave it.

Cover the burn with a dry sterile dressing. And that is all that goes on it. No ointment, no cream, no antiseptic, no butter, no toothpaste, no ice. Everything in that list has been applied by somebody before your arrival, and all of them either trap heat, cause harm, or have to be painfully scrubbed off before anybody can assess the burn properly.

Do not break blisters. The blister roof is intact skin and it is a barrier against infection. It will be dealt with properly later by somebody who can do it cleanly.

Keep the patient warm, and take it seriously. A burn patient has lost the organ that holds heat in, and they will become cold faster than you expect — especially after cooling, especially undressed, especially in winter. Blankets, heat the ambulance, and do it before they start shivering.

And this one matters as much as anything: look for the other injuries. A burn is visually overwhelming. It pulls every pair of eyes in the room towards it, and meanwhile the patient has a fractured ankle from jumping out of a window and a head injury from the beam that came down. People escaping fires fall, jump and get hit by things. Work your normal assessment rather than treating the burn as the whole patient.

Some burns are significant regardless of how small they are. Face, because of the airway and the eyes. Hands and feet, because of function. Genitalia. Any burn crossing a joint, because scarring restricts movement permanently. And circumferential burns, which constrict. A small burn in any of those places is not a small burn.

Age matters too. The very young and the very old do worse with the same percentage burn than a healthy adult.

The actual burn centre criteria — which percentages, which depths, which ages — are set locally and by your regional burn service. I am not giving figures here because they differ and they get revised. Learn yours.

And one last thing, which is uncomfortable and necessary. Consider whether the burn matches the story. Burns are a common presentation of abuse in children and vulnerable adults. A pattern that does not fit the history — a glove or stocking distribution, a clean edge, a shape that matches an object, a delay in seeking help, an account that keeps changing — is something you record factually and report through your safeguarding route. Describe exactly what you saw and exactly what you were told. Do not accuse anybody, and do not decide not to mention it because you might be wrong.
read.standard: Following cessation of the burning process, management comprises early removal of rings, jewellery and constricting items before oedema precludes it; adherent material is left in situ with surrounding fabric cut away. Burns are covered with dry sterile dressings; topical preparations, including ointments, creams, antiseptics and domestic applications, are contraindicated, as is ice. Blisters are not deroofed, intact epidermis constituting an infection barrier. Hypothermia develops rapidly owing to loss of integumentary thermoregulation, particularly following cooling, and active warming is prioritised. Concurrent injuries must be sought, as the visual prominence of burns distracts from fractures, haemorrhage and head injury sustained during escape. Burns involving the face, hands, feet, genitalia, or crossing joints, and circumferential burns, are significant irrespective of extent. Paediatric and geriatric patients sustain greater physiological insult at equivalent extent. Burn centre referral criteria are established locally and by regional burn services. Non-accidental injury should be considered where the burn pattern is inconsistent with the stated mechanism, with factual documentation and safeguarding referral per local policy.

eli_new.analogy: A burn takes up the whole room. The fractured ankle from jumping out of the window does not, and it is still there.
eli_new.body: Take the rings off first. It takes fifteen seconds, and in ten minutes it will be impossible — at which point a wedding ring is a tourniquet on a finger that is already injured.

concepts.title: Fractures, dislocations, sprains and strains
key_points: A fracture is a broken bone; a dislocation is a joint out of position; a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament; a strain is a stretched or torn muscle or tendon
You cannot reliably tell a fracture from a sprain in the field — treat what you cannot exclude as a fracture
An open fracture is one where the skin over it is broken, whether or not bone is visible; it carries a high infection risk
Signs are deformity, swelling, bruising, tenderness over the bone, inability to use the limb, and crepitus — which you never deliberately elicit
Compare with the other side: a limb is its own best reference
Dislocations are extremely painful and frequently threaten the nerves and vessels crossing that joint
Angulated fractures and dislocations are splinted in the position found, unless the limb is pulseless — then follow your protocol
A femur fracture can bleed a significant volume into the thigh, so it is a circulation problem as well as a bone problem
Check circulation, sensation and movement before splinting and again after, every time
misconceptions: Trying to distinguish a sprain from a fracture in the field
Testing for crepitus deliberately
Treating a femur fracture as purely an orthopaedic problem
Splinting without checking circulation first
exam_favorites: Cannot tell a fracture from a sprain in the field

read.plain:
Four words that get mixed up, and the distinction is simpler than it sounds.

A fracture is a broken bone. A dislocation is a joint where the bones have come out of position. A sprain is a ligament — the tissue joining bone to bone across a joint — stretched or torn. A strain is a muscle or tendon stretched or torn.

Now the practical truth: you cannot reliably tell a fracture from a sprain at the roadside. Neither can most doctors without an x-ray. Swollen, painful, bruised ankles are fractures often enough that guessing is not worth doing. So the rule is straightforward — treat what you cannot exclude as a fracture, splint it, and let the x-ray sort it out. Nobody has been harmed by a splinted sprain.

An open fracture is one where the skin over the fracture is broken. Note that carefully: it does not require visible bone. A small puncture wound over a fracture site, made by a bone end that went out and came back, makes that an open fracture, and it carries a high infection risk that changes how urgently it is managed. Cover it with a sterile dressing, note it, and say the word open at handover.

The signs: deformity, swelling, bruising, tenderness directly over the bone, an inability to use or bear weight on the limb, and crepitus — the grating of bone ends.

On crepitus: you may feel it while doing something else, and if you do, that is a finding. You never go looking for it. Deliberately moving a limb to see whether it grates causes pain and further damage for information that changes nothing about your treatment.

Use the other side. Patients come with a built-in reference. Compare shape, length, alignment, colour and warmth against the uninjured limb — subtle deformity is far easier to see in comparison than in isolation.

Dislocations deserve respect. They are ferociously painful, and because nerves and vessels cross joints, a displaced joint can stretch or compress them. Check circulation and sensation distal to any dislocation immediately, and again after any movement.

As a general rule, splint angulated fractures and dislocations in the position you found them. Straightening things causes damage and pain. The exception is a limb with no pulse below the injury, where restoring perfusion may justify a single careful attempt at realignment — and that is a protocol matter, so know what yours says before you are standing over a white foot.

One fracture deserves separate mention. A femur can bleed a substantial volume into the thigh, and two femurs can produce shock on their own. Treat a femur fracture as a circulation problem as well as a bone problem, and take a pulse rather than just a splint.

And the habit that underpins all of this: circulation, sensation and movement below the injury, checked before you splint and again after. Every time, recorded both times. It is the only way anybody knows whether your splint helped or harmed.
read.standard: Fracture denotes osseous discontinuity; dislocation denotes articular displacement; sprain denotes ligamentous stretching or tearing; strain denotes musculotendinous stretching or tearing. Prehospital differentiation of fracture from sprain is unreliable; injuries that cannot be excluded as fracture are managed as such. Open fracture denotes disruption of overlying integument irrespective of bone visibility, conferring substantial infection risk and altering urgency; sterile covering and explicit handover are indicated. Findings include deformity, swelling, ecchymosis, point tenderness, functional loss and crepitus; crepitus is never deliberately elicited, as provocation produces pain and further injury without altering management. Contralateral comparison provides an internal reference for subtle deformity. Dislocations produce severe pain and may compromise neurovascular structures crossing the joint, requiring immediate and repeated distal assessment. Angulated fractures and dislocations are splinted in the position found; absent distal pulse may justify a single careful realignment attempt per protocol. Femoral fracture may sequester substantial blood volume within the thigh and constitutes a circulatory as well as skeletal injury. Circulation, sensation and movement distal to injury are assessed and documented before and after splinting.

eli_new.analogy: A patient brings their own control group. The other arm is the same arm without the injury, and comparing the two shows you things staring at one never will.

concepts.title: Splinting principles and types
key_points: Splinting reduces pain, prevents further damage to nerves and vessels, limits bleeding, and makes movement possible
Immobilise the joint above and the joint below the fracture; for a joint injury, immobilise the bone above and below
Check circulation, sensation and movement before splinting and again immediately after — every single time
Expose the injury and cover any open wound with a sterile dressing before the splint goes on
Pad the splint and pad the gaps, especially over bony points, because pressure under a splint causes injury over time
Splint in the position found, unless the limb is pulseless and your protocol permits realignment
Rigid splints, formable splints, vacuum splints, sling and swathe, and the patient's own body all have a place
Splint before moving the patient where the situation allows, but a critical patient is moved and splinted en route
Do not delay transport of a major trauma patient to splint individual fractures

Failing to pad bony points
Splinting individual fractures on a major trauma patient before transport

read.plain:
Splinting does four things. It reduces pain, often dramatically. It stops broken ends moving and causing more damage to the nerves and vessels beside them. It limits bleeding, because moving bone ends tear tissue and keep bleeding going. And it makes the patient movable, which they may not be otherwise.

The basic rule of coverage: for a fracture in a bone, immobilise the joint above and the joint below it. For an injury to a joint, immobilise the bone above and the bone below. Splinting just the painful spot leaves the ends free to move, which defeats the purpose.

Then the rule that matters more than any technique: circulation, sensation and movement, before and after. Before, so you know what you started with. After, so you know your splint has not made it worse. A splint applied over a limb that already had no pulse is a different situation from a splint that caused the pulse to disappear, and the only way anybody can tell those apart is if you checked first. Record both.

Before the splint goes on: expose the injury properly and cover any open wound with a sterile dressing. You cannot dress a wound through a splint, and discovering an open fracture after immobilising the limb means undoing your own work.

Pad it. Pad the splint itself and pad the gaps between splint and limb, particularly over bony points — ankles, knees, elbows, wrists. A hard surface pressing on a bony point for forty minutes of transport causes real injury, and the patient may not be able to tell you because of the pain from the fracture. Padding is not a nicety.

Splint in the position found. Straightening angulated fractures causes damage and severe pain. The exception is a limb with no pulse below the injury — where restoring circulation may justify one careful attempt at realignment, and where your protocol governs. Know what yours says.

The types available: rigid splints, which are firm and need the limb brought to them or padding to fill the gaps; formable splints, which mould to the limb as found and are excellent for angulated injuries; vacuum splints, which conform closely and hold the position found extremely well; slings and swathes for the shoulder and upper arm; and the patient themselves — an injured leg splinted to the good leg, an injured arm bound to the chest — which works when equipment is short or the patient must be moved now.

Finally, timing, which is where judgement comes in. For an isolated limb injury in a stable patient, splint before you move them. It is kinder and it prevents further damage.

For a major trauma patient, do not do that. Splinting individual fractures on somebody who is bleeding internally spends the minutes that matter most on the least important injury. Get them onto a device that immobilises everything at once, get moving, and splint en route if at all. A femur fracture in a patient with a rigid abdomen is not what is going to kill them.
read.standard: Splinting reduces pain, prevents further neurovascular injury from bone end movement, limits haemorrhage and facilitates patient movement. Immobilisation encompasses the joint proximal and distal to a fractured bone, or the bone proximal and distal to an injured joint. Circulation, sensation and movement are assessed and documented immediately before and immediately after application, permitting differentiation between pre-existing and splint-induced compromise. Injuries are exposed and open wounds covered with sterile dressings prior to splint application. Padding of the splint and of gaps, particularly over bony prominences, prevents pressure injury during transport, which the patient may not report owing to fracture pain. Splinting is performed in the position found; realignment is reserved for pulseless limbs where protocol permits. Splint types comprise rigid, formable, vacuum, sling and swathe, and anatomical splinting using the patient's own body. In isolated injury with a stable patient, splinting precedes movement; in major trauma, whole-body immobilisation and expedited transport take precedence, with individual splinting performed en route or omitted.

eli_new.analogy: A splint has two jobs: hold the ends still, and do no harm for the next forty minutes. The padding is the second job.
eli_new.body: The judgement call is timing. For a broken wrist, splint then move. For a patient with a rigid abdomen and a broken femur, the femur can wait — spending five minutes on it is spending five minutes on the injury least likely to kill them.

concepts.title: The traction splint
key_points: A traction splint is for an isolated closed mid-shaft femur fracture, and for almost nothing else
It works by applying steady pull along the line of the bone, which realigns the ends and relaxes the powerful thigh muscles that are pulling them past each other
That muscle spasm is what causes the extreme pain and the ongoing bleeding, so relieving it treats both
It is contraindicated with injury to the pelvis, hip, knee or ankle on that side, with a lower leg fracture, and with a partial amputation or avulsion
It is not used in an open femur fracture where bone would be drawn back inside, per protocol
Applying traction to a fractured pelvis can worsen the bleeding, which is why the pelvis must be assessed first
Check circulation, sensation and movement before and after, as with any splint
Two people apply it: one maintains manual traction throughout while the other works the device
Manual traction is never released once started until the device has taken over
misconceptions: Applying it with a suspected pelvic fracture
Releasing manual traction part way through application
Using it for a fracture near the knee or ankle
Using it on a patient with multiple injuries who needs to move now
exam_favorites: Why it relieves pain and bleeding

read.plain:
The traction splint has one job and a narrow set of circumstances for doing it: an isolated, closed, mid-shaft femur fracture.

Here is why it works. The thigh contains the most powerful muscles in the body, and when the femur breaks, those muscles contract. They pull the broken ends past each other and hold them there, overlapping. That spasm is what causes the extreme pain of a femur fracture, it shortens the limb, and it keeps bone ends grinding through tissue and bleeding.

Applying steady traction along the line of the bone overcomes that pull. The ends come back into alignment, the muscles relax, the pain falls substantially, and the bleeding slows because the ends stop moving. It is one of the more satisfying things you can do, and one of the few interventions where the patient thanks you immediately.

Now the contraindications, which is where this concept earns its difficulty.

Any injury to the pelvis, hip, knee or ankle on that side. Any fracture of the lower leg. A partial amputation or avulsion where traction could pull the limb apart. And an open femur fracture where traction would draw contaminated bone back inside — follow your protocol on that one, as practice varies.

The pelvis matters most. Traction pulls on the femur and the femur pulls on the pelvis, so applying traction to a patient with a fractured pelvis can pull open a pelvic fracture that is already bleeding heavily. That is why the pelvis is assessed before the traction splint comes off the vehicle, and why the sequence is not negotiable.

The logic of the contraindications is the same in each case: traction is a pulling force, and it needs somewhere solid to pull against at each end. If either anchor is broken, you are pulling a broken thing apart.

Application is a two-person job and cannot properly be done alone. One person applies manual traction and holds it. The other measures, positions and works the device. Then the device takes over and only then does the first person let go.

That last point is the one to remember. Once manual traction starts, it is not released until the mechanical traction is applied and holding. Letting go part way lets the muscles snap the ends back past each other, which hurts enormously, undoes what you achieved, and causes more damage on the way.

And as with every splint: circulation, sensation and movement before, and again after.

One judgement note. This is an excellent device for the right patient, and the right patient is a stable one with an isolated femur fracture. In a multiply injured patient who needs to be moving now, it is usually the wrong use of five minutes.
read.standard: The traction splint is indicated for isolated closed mid-shaft femoral fracture. Mechanism relies on countering spasm of the powerful thigh musculature, which following fracture contracts and displaces the bone ends into overlap, producing severe pain, limb shortening and continued haemorrhage from bone end movement. Applied longitudinal traction restores alignment, relieves spasm, reduces pain and limits haemorrhage. Contraindications comprise injury to the ipsilateral pelvis, hip, knee or ankle; fracture of the lower leg; partial amputation or avulsion where traction risks separation; and open femoral fracture where traction would retract contaminated bone, per protocol. Pelvic fracture is the critical contraindication, as femoral traction transmits force to the pelvis and may distract an actively haemorrhaging pelvic fracture; pelvic assessment therefore precedes application. Application requires two providers: one maintains manual traction continuously while the second applies the device. Manual traction is not released until mechanical traction is established, as premature release permits recurrence of overlap with associated pain and tissue damage. Circulation, sensation and movement are assessed before and after. Application is inappropriate in multiply injured patients requiring expedited transport.

eli_new.analogy: The thigh muscles are strong enough to pull a broken femur past itself and hold it there. Traction is you having a quiet argument with the strongest muscles in the body, and winning by being steady rather than strong.
eli_new.body: Every contraindication is the same idea: traction pulls between two anchors, and if an anchor is broken you are pulling a broken thing apart. Pelvis, hip, knee, ankle, lower leg, partial amputation — all of them are a broken anchor.

concepts.title: Pelvic fractures
key_points: The pelvis is a ring, and a ring cannot break in only one place — one visible fracture means another somewhere else
A major pelvic fracture can bleed enormously, because large vessels run across the pelvis and the space has no limit to fill
Bleeding from a pelvic fracture is internal, invisible, and not reachable by anything an EMT carries
Suspect it from the mechanism: a fall from height, a motorcyclist, a pedestrian struck, a crash with side intrusion, and a fall from standing in an older patient
Signs are pelvic pain, instability, bruising over the pelvis or perineum, leg length difference or outward rotation, and unexplained shock
Assess pelvic stability ONCE, gently, and never again — repeated springing disturbs clot and worsens bleeding
Many services no longer test stability at all and rely on mechanism and pain; know what yours says
Do not log roll a patient with a suspected pelvic fracture if it can be avoided; use a scoop or a flat lift
The treatment is a pelvic binder, applied early, plus warmth, minimal movement and rapid transport
misconceptions: Springing the pelvis repeatedly to confirm instability
Log rolling a patient with a suspected pelvic fracture
Waiting for a low blood pressure before suspecting pelvic bleeding
Treating a fall from standing in an older patient as a minor mechanism
exam_favorites: A ring breaks in two places
Assess stability once, or not at all

read.plain:
The pelvis is a ring of bone. That single fact explains most of what follows.

A ring cannot break in only one place. Take a metal ring and try to break it once — it does not work, it either holds or it gives way in two places. So if you find or suspect one pelvic fracture, there is another, and the ring has come apart in a way that lets the two halves move independently.

Why that matters is what runs across the pelvis. Large vessels, a rich network of veins, and the bone itself is highly vascular. When the ring comes apart, all of that tears. And because the pelvis has opened up, the space available for blood to fill has grown — there is no ceiling on it. Patients exsanguinate into their own pelvis.

Every bit of that bleeding is internal. You cannot see it, cannot measure it, and cannot put pressure on it. This is why the mechanism-plus-shock combination matters so much: a patient with the right mechanism and unexplained shock has a pelvic fracture until somebody images them, regardless of what your hands find.

Mechanisms: a fall from height. A motorcyclist. A pedestrian struck by a vehicle. A crash with intrusion from the side. And — the one that gets overlooked — a fall from standing height in an older person, which fractures pelvises routinely and does not feel like a mechanism at all.

Signs: pain in the pelvis, groin or lower back. Instability if you assess for it. Bruising over the pelvis or perineum. One leg shorter, or rotated outwards. Blood at the urethra. And shock with no other explanation.

Now, assessing stability. If your protocol has you check it: once. Gently. Downwards and inwards pressure on the iliac crests, one time, and then never again. The reason is mechanical — whatever clot has formed across those torn vessels is fragile, and springing the pelvis breaks it up and restarts the bleeding. The check tells you something you probably already knew from the mechanism, and each repetition costs blood.

And be aware that many services have moved away from testing stability at all, on exactly that reasoning — the test can harm and rarely changes the decision. Mechanism and pain are enough to act on. Know what your protocol says.

Movement matters too. Do not log roll a patient with a suspected pelvic fracture if there is any alternative. Rolling twists the two halves of a broken ring against each other. Use a scoop stretcher, or a flat lift with enough hands, and move them once.

The treatment is a pelvic binder, applied early — which has its own concept — along with keeping them warm, moving them as little as possible, and going quickly.
read.standard: The pelvis constitutes an osseous ring; ring structures cannot sustain single-point disruption, so identification of one fracture implies a second. Disruption produces haemorrhage from adjacent major vessels, the pelvic venous plexus and cancellous bone, into a retroperitoneal space whose volume increases with displacement, permitting exsanguinating haemorrhage. Haemorrhage is entirely internal and inaccessible to prehospital control. Mechanisms conferring suspicion include falls from height, motorcyclist and pedestrian impacts, lateral compartment intrusion, and ground-level falls in geriatric patients. Findings include pelvic, groin or lumbar pain, instability, ecchymosis over the pelvis or perineum, limb shortening or external rotation, urethral bleeding, and unexplained shock. Where protocol directs stability assessment, it is performed once only with gentle downward and inward compression of the iliac crests; repeated assessment disrupts clot and increases haemorrhage. Many services have discontinued stability testing on this basis, relying on mechanism and pain. Log rolling is avoided where alternatives exist, as rotation displaces ring segments against one another; scoop stretcher or flat lift with adequate personnel is preferred. Management comprises early pelvic binder application, normothermia, minimal movement and expedited transport.

eli_new.analogy: You cannot break a ring in one place. If you have found one fracture, there is a second one you have not found, and the ring is now two pieces that can move.
eli_new.body: Assess the pelvis once, or not at all. Every spring of an unstable pelvis breaks up whatever clot had formed, and the test rarely tells you something the mechanism had not already told you.

story.title: Spring it again
story.dispatch: Debrief — pelvic fracture, three crew members on scene.
story.body:
The first crew member checked the pelvis and found it unstable, and said so.

The second checked, to confirm. The third checked, because they had not felt one before and wanted to know what it felt like.

Whatever clot had formed across those torn veins was broken up three separate times, by three people all doing something they believed was reasonable.

concepts.title: Neurovascular checks and compartment syndrome
key_points: Every limb injury gets a neurovascular check before and after anything you do to it
The check is remembered as CSM — circulation, sensation, movement — or PMS, pulse, motor, sensory
Circulation: pulse if findable, skin colour, warmth, and capillary refill compared with the other side
Sensation: can they feel you touching, and does it feel the same as the other limb
Movement: can they wiggle fingers or toes, within the limits of the pain
A finding is only useful compared against something — the other limb, or your own earlier check
Record the time with each check, because what matters is whether it changed and when
Compartment syndrome is the reason these checks are not paperwork: pain out of proportion is the earliest sign, and a present pulse excludes nothing
If anything has worsened after a splint or bandage, loosen it and reassess before you go anywhere
misconceptions: Recording 'CSM intact' without recording a time
Checking before but not after an intervention
Being reassured by a present pulse in a limb with severe pain
Leaving a splint on when circulation worsened after applying it
exam_favorites: Compare against the other limb and your earlier check

read.plain:
Neurovascular checks are the most repeated and most skipped assessment in trauma. Everybody knows to do them; a lot of records say 'CSM intact' with no time and no detail, and that record is worth very little.

The check has three parts, remembered either as CSM — circulation, sensation, movement — or PMS — pulse, motor, sensory. Same thing.

Circulation. A pulse distal to the injury if you can find one, and often you cannot, which is fine. Then colour: pink, pale, dusky, mottled. Warmth, felt with the back of your hand. And capillary refill, pressed and released, compared with the other side.

Sensation. Touch them and ask whether they can feel it, and then ask the better question: does it feel the same as the other hand or foot? Patients frequently say yes to 'can you feel this' and then, asked to compare, say the injured side feels duller or tingly. That comparison is where the finding is.

Movement. Can they wiggle fingers or toes? Not move the injured joint — just the digits beyond the injury. Pain limits this and that is expected; you are looking for whether the ability is there at all.

The thread through all of it is comparison. A capillary refill of three seconds means one thing if the other hand is two and quite another if the other hand is also three. A single reading without a comparison is nearly uninterpretable, and you have two comparisons available: the other limb, and your own previous check.

Which is why times matter. 'CSM intact' tells the hospital almost nothing. 'Radial pulse present, fingers pink and warm, sensation equal, moving all fingers — 14:20. Repeated after splint 14:26, unchanged' tells them everything, and it tells them your splint did no harm. If it later changes, somebody can see exactly when.

And the reason all this matters rather than being paperwork: compartment syndrome. Swelling inside a compartment that cannot expand raises the pressure until muscle starts dying, with intact skin and an unremarkable-looking limb.

The earliest sign is pain out of proportion to the apparent injury. A patient whose pain seems excessive for what you can see is giving you a finding. Pain on passive stretching of the fingers or toes, a tight woody feel to the muscle compartment, and later numbness and tingling follow.

The pulse is the trap. It is often still present, because arterial pressure is higher than the pressure that has already shut down the small vessels feeding the muscle. Losing the pulse is a very late sign, and finding one present is no reassurance at all. If you wait for a pulseless limb before taking the pain seriously, the muscle has been dying for hours.

And the practical consequence: if anything is worse after you applied a splint or a bandage, loosen it and reassess before moving. Not at the hospital. Now.
read.standard: Neurovascular assessment is performed distal to every limb injury before and after any intervention, denoted CSM (circulation, sensation, movement) or PMS (pulse, motor, sensory). Circulatory assessment comprises distal pulse where palpable, colour, temperature and capillary refill with contralateral comparison. Sensory assessment establishes not only presence of sensation but equivalence to the contralateral limb, comparison frequently revealing deficit that presence alone does not. Motor assessment establishes digital movement distal to injury within pain limits. Findings require comparison, either contralateral or against prior assessment; isolated values are largely uninterpretable. Documentation includes timing, as change and its timing constitute the clinically significant information. Compartment syndrome represents the rationale for serial assessment: raised intracompartmental pressure produces muscle necrosis with intact integument. The earliest finding is pain disproportionate to apparent injury, followed by pain on passive stretch, a tense compartment, and later paraesthesia. Distal pulses commonly remain palpable, as arterial pressure exceeds the capillary closing pressure already reached; pulselessness is a late finding and preserved pulses provide no reassurance. Deterioration following splint or bandage application requires immediate loosening and reassessment.

eli_new.analogy: A single capillary refill reading is a word with no sentence around it. The other limb and your own earlier check are the sentence.
eli_new.body: Write the time. 'CSM intact' with no time is almost worthless; the same words with a time, repeated after your splint, prove your splint did no harm and let anyone afterwards see exactly when something changed.

story.title: CSM intact
story.dispatch: Handover — forearm fracture, splinted at scene, transport 35 minutes.
story.body:
The record said 'CSM intact' and nothing else. No time, no detail, no second check.

At hospital the fingers were cool and the patient could not feel a pinch on the little finger.

Nobody could say whether that had happened in the splint, before it, or on the way in. Two lines and two times would have answered it.

S — Sensation: not just 'can you feel this' but 'does it feel the SAME as the other side?'

BEFORE and AFTER every splint, bandage or movement. WITH A TIME on each.

concepts.title: Pelvic binder application
key_points: A pelvic binder closes the pelvic ring, reducing the space blood can fill and allowing clot to form
It is applied for a suspected pelvic fracture based on mechanism and findings — you do not need confirmation to apply it
The single most common error is placing it too high: it goes over the greater trochanters, not over the iliac crests or the waist
The greater trochanters are the bony points at the widest part of the hips, and the binder is centred on them
Remove objects from pockets before applying, because anything trapped underneath becomes a pressure point for hours
Apply it early, before moving the patient where possible, and use a scoop or a flat lift rather than a log roll
Tighten to the manufacturer's specification — more is not better and over-tightening can cause harm
Once applied, it stays on: do not remove it to examine the pelvis, and do not loosen it to check
A folded sheet can be used where no commercial device is available, per protocol, applied at the same level
misconceptions: Applying the binder over the iliac crests or the waist
Log rolling the patient to apply it
Removing or loosening it to examine the pelvis
Leaving keys or a phone in a pocket underneath it
Waiting for confirmation of a fracture before applying it
exam_favorites: Over the greater trochanters, not the crests
Apply early and leave it on

read.plain:
A pelvic binder closes the ring. When the pelvis comes apart the space available to fill with blood increases, and bringing the two halves back together reduces that space and lets clot form and hold. It also stops the broken ends grinding, which is both painful and a source of continued bleeding.

You apply it on suspicion. You do not need a confirmed fracture, you will not get one in the field, and waiting for certainty is waiting for blood loss. Mechanism plus pain, or mechanism plus unexplained shock, is enough.

Now the error that matters more than all the others: position.

A pelvic binder goes over the greater trochanters — the bony prominences you can feel at the widest part of the hips, roughly level with the crease of the buttock, considerably lower than most people place it. It does not go over the iliac crests, the bony ridges you feel when you put your hands on somebody's hips. And it certainly does not go around the waist.

A binder placed too high does not close the ring. It compresses the top of the pelvis, which can actually open the bottom of it, and it is worse than not applying one. If you learn one thing from this concept: lower than you think. Find the trochanters with your hands and centre the binder on them.

Before it goes on, empty the pockets. Keys, a phone, a wallet, a belt buckle — anything trapped underneath will sit under pressure against skin for hours, because this binder is not coming off before hospital, and possibly not for some time afterwards. Pressure injuries from objects under binders are a documented and entirely preventable harm.

Apply it early, and apply it before moving the patient where the situation allows — the movement is what displaces an unstable pelvis. Getting it on first means one less opportunity for harm.

Getting it under the patient is the practical problem. Do not log roll if there is any alternative. Rolling twists the two halves of the ring against each other. Slide the binder under the natural hollow at the knees and work it up, or use a scoop stretcher, or a flat lift with enough hands. Move the patient once.

Tighten to the manufacturer's specification — many devices have a mechanism that indicates correct tension. More is not better. Over-tightening can damage skin and, with certain fracture patterns, cause harm.

And once it is on, it stays on. Do not remove it to examine the pelvis. Do not loosen it to check whether it is working. Do not take it off for the x-ray — that is a hospital decision made with surgeons present. Every removal is a fresh opportunity to restart bleeding that had stopped.

If no commercial binder is available, a folded sheet applied at the same level and secured can be used per protocol. The level is the part that matters; the material is secondary.
read.standard: A pelvic binder approximates the disrupted pelvic ring, reducing potential space for haemorrhage and permitting clot stabilisation, while limiting bone end movement. Application is based on suspicion derived from mechanism with pain or unexplained shock; radiographic confirmation is neither available nor required prehospitally. Correct placement is centred over the greater trochanters, at the widest point of the hips, substantially lower than intuitive placement. Application over the iliac crests or the waist fails to close the ring, may distract the inferior pelvis, and is worse than no application. Pockets are emptied prior to application, as retained objects produce pressure injury during prolonged application. Early application preceding patient movement is preferred, as movement displaces the unstable ring. Log rolling is avoided; the device is slid beneath the popliteal hollow and worked proximally, or a scoop stretcher or flat lift employed. Tensioning follows manufacturer specification, over-tightening producing skin injury and potential harm with certain fracture patterns. The binder is not removed or loosened prehospitally for examination or assessment; removal is a hospital decision. A folded sheet applied at the same anatomical level may substitute per protocol.

concepts.title: Skull fractures and scalp wounds
key_points: Scalp wounds bleed dramatically because the scalp has a rich blood supply and the vessels do not retract well
That bleeding can be significant, particularly in children and in anticoagulated patients
Control scalp bleeding with direct pressure, but not firm pressure over a suspected depressed or open skull fracture
Never probe a scalp wound with fingers or instruments, because you may push fragments inward
A basilar skull fracture is a fracture at the base of the skull and has characteristic late signs
Bruising behind the ear, called Battle sign, and bruising around both eyes, called raccoon eyes, appear hours after the injury and their absence early means nothing
Clear or blood-stained fluid from the ear or nose may be cerebrospinal fluid and suggests a basilar fracture

Any skull fracture means force reached the brain, so the brain injury underneath matters more than the bone
misconceptions: Packing a draining ear or nose
Probing a scalp wound
Pressing hard over a depressed skull fracture

read.plain:
Scalp wounds bleed far more than they should, and there is a reason. The scalp has an unusually rich blood supply, and its vessels are held open by the fibrous tissue around them, so they cannot retract and constrict the way vessels elsewhere do. A small scalp laceration produces a genuinely alarming quantity of blood.

Usually it looks worse than it is. But not always: in a small child, whose total blood volume is modest, and in anybody on an anticoagulant, a scalp wound can cause significant blood loss. Do not dismiss it simply because scalp wounds are famous for looking dramatic.

Control it with direct pressure, with one important caution. If you suspect a depressed or open skull fracture underneath — if you can feel a step, a soft boggy area, or anything that moves — do not press hard on it. Use gentle pressure around the edges instead, and control what you can without pushing anything inward.

And never probe a scalp wound. Not with a finger, not with an instrument, not to see how deep it is. If there are bone fragments, probing pushes them towards the brain. Cover it, apply appropriate pressure, and leave the exploration to people with imaging.

A basilar skull fracture is a fracture through the base of the skull, and it has a set of signs worth knowing precisely because of when they appear.

Battle sign is bruising over the mastoid, behind the ear. Raccoon eyes is bruising around both eyes, without direct injury to them. Both are real and both are useful — and both take hours to develop. They are more often seen in the emergency department than in the field. So finding neither tells you nothing at all about whether there is a basilar fracture; if the mechanism fits, suspect it anyway.

The finding you may actually see is fluid. Clear or blood-tinged fluid draining from the ear or the nose after head trauma can be cerebrospinal fluid, escaping through a fracture at the skull base. Blood that appears diluted, or has a clear ring around it on a dressing, points the same way.

What you do about that is specific: nothing that blocks it. Do not pack the ear. Do not pack the nose. Cover loosely with a dressing that absorbs without obstructing, and let it drain. Packing raises the pressure inside the skull and can drive contamination inward through the fracture, towards the brain and the fluid around it.

And hold onto the last point, which puts the rest in perspective. A skull fracture matters mainly because it tells you how much force reached the head. The bone itself is rarely what harms the patient; the brain underneath it is. A patient with an obvious skull fracture and a normal level of consciousness may do well. A patient with no fracture at all and a falling level of consciousness is in far more trouble.
read.standard: Scalp lacerations produce disproportionate haemorrhage owing to rich vascularity and fibrous tethering of vessels preventing retraction and vasoconstriction. Loss may be clinically significant in paediatric patients and those receiving anticoagulation. Haemorrhage control employs direct pressure, modified to peripheral gentle pressure where depressed or open skull fracture is suspected. Wound probing is contraindicated owing to risk of intracranial displacement of fragments. Basilar skull fracture presents with retroauricular ecchymosis (Battle sign) and periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes), both developing over hours and therefore frequently absent prehospitally; early absence carries no exclusionary value. Otorrhoea or rhinorrhoea of clear or blood-tinged fluid suggests cerebrospinal fluid leak through a basilar fracture, with a halo appearance on absorbent dressing. Aural and nasal packing are contraindicated, raising intracranial pressure and risking retrograde contamination; loose absorbent covering permitting drainage is indicated. Skull fracture principally indicates transmitted force; underlying cerebral injury determines outcome, and absence of fracture does not indicate absence of brain injury.

concepts.title: Traumatic brain injury, Cushing triad and herniation
key_points: The skull is a closed box: once the brain swells or blood collects, something has to give and the pressure rises
Primary brain injury is the damage done at the moment of impact and cannot be undone
Secondary brain injury is the damage that follows — from low oxygen, low blood pressure, rising pressure inside the skull — and preventing it is the entire prehospital job
The two things that most worsen outcome are hypoxia and hypotension, so oxygenation and perfusion are the treatment
A falling level of consciousness is the single most important sign, and repeated assessments matter more than any one
The Cushing triad is rising blood pressure, falling pulse rate and irregular breathing, and it is a late sign of dangerously raised pressure
Herniation signs include a fixed dilated pupil, usually on the same side as the injury, and posturing or a rapid fall in consciousness
Vomiting, seizures and worsening headache all suggest rising pressure
Keep the head neutral and elevated per protocol, avoid anything that raises pressure further, and transport quickly with a pre-alert
misconceptions: Treating a single normal assessment as reassurance
Waiting for the Cushing triad before acting
Allowing hypoxia or hypotension in a head-injured patient
Hyperventilating routinely rather than per protocol
exam_favorites: Hypoxia and hypotension are the enemies
Repeated assessments beat any single one

read.plain:
The skull is a closed box with a fixed volume, containing brain, blood and cerebrospinal fluid. Add anything — swelling, a collection of blood — and there is nowhere for it to go. The pressure inside rises, and rising pressure squeezes the brain against the inside of its own container.

That gives us the most useful distinction in head injury.

Primary brain injury is what happened at the moment of impact: bruising, tearing, shearing of tissue. It is done. Nothing anybody does afterwards changes it.

Secondary brain injury is everything that happens after — injury caused by low oxygen, low blood pressure, rising intracranial pressure, high or low carbon dioxide, high temperature, seizures. That damage has not happened yet when you arrive, and preventing it is the entire prehospital job.

This is genuinely one of the places where an EMT changes outcomes. Two things worsen head injury outcome more than anything else: hypoxia and hypotension. A brain that is swelling and under pressure needs oxygen and needs blood arriving. Let the saturation drop or the blood pressure fall and the brain is injured further, on top of what the impact did.

So the treatment is unglamorous and enormously effective. Keep the airway clear. Keep the oxygen up. Support ventilation if it is inadequate — at a normal rate, not fast, unless your protocol directs otherwise for signs of herniation. And treat any other cause of low blood pressure aggressively, because that bleeding leg is now also a brain problem.

The most important sign is the level of consciousness, and specifically whether it is changing. One assessment is a data point; three assessments are a trend, and the trend is what matters. A patient who was alert and is now confused has deteriorated even if they are still talking. Record each assessment with a time.

The Cushing triad is the classic teaching sign of dangerously raised intracranial pressure: blood pressure going up, pulse rate coming down, and breathing becoming irregular. Learn it, recognise it — and understand that it is a late sign. By the time it is present the pressure has been rising for some time. It confirms what a falling level of consciousness told you earlier. Do not wait for it.

Herniation is the brain being forced through the openings in the skull, and it is catastrophic. The signs: a pupil that becomes fixed and dilated, usually on the same side as the injury; a rapid fall in consciousness; and posturing, where the limbs adopt rigid abnormal positions in response to stimulus. Vomiting, seizures and a worsening headache all point at rising pressure too.

Practically: keep the head in a neutral position and elevate it per protocol. Avoid anything that raises pressure further — constriction around the neck, rough handling, letting them strain. Keep them warm, treat seizures per protocol, and transport quickly with a pre-alert. A patient with signs of rising pressure needs a neurosurgical centre, and that decision is made faster if you say so on the radio.
read.standard: The cranial vault is a fixed-volume compartment containing brain, blood and cerebrospinal fluid; addition of oedema or haematoma raises intracranial pressure. Primary brain injury denotes damage sustained at impact and is not modifiable. Secondary brain injury denotes subsequent damage from hypoxia, hypotension, raised intracranial pressure, abnormal carbon dioxide, hyperthermia and seizure activity; its prevention constitutes the prehospital objective. Hypoxia and hypotension are the principal determinants of worsened outcome, rendering oxygenation and perfusion the primary interventions. Ventilatory support is provided at normal rate unless protocol directs otherwise for herniation signs. Serial assessment of level of consciousness provides the most significant clinical information, trend exceeding any single measurement in value; assessments are documented with times. The Cushing triad — hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration — indicates critically raised intracranial pressure and is a late finding confirming earlier deterioration in consciousness. Herniation manifests as ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, rapid decline in consciousness and abnormal posturing. Vomiting, seizures and progressive headache indicate rising pressure. Management comprises neutral head positioning with elevation per protocol, avoidance of cervical constriction and straining, normothermia, seizure management per protocol, and expedited transport to neurosurgical capability with prearrival notification.

eli_new.analogy: The impact is a fire that has already happened. Everything you do is stopping the sprinklers from failing while somebody drives to the building.
eli_new.body: The single most valuable thing in a head injury is repeated assessment of consciousness with times on it. Not the pupils, not the Cushing triad — those come late. A patient going from alert to confused over twenty minutes is the finding, and it only exists if somebody checked twice.
