concepts.title: Concussion
key_points: A concussion is a brain injury caused by force transmitted to the head, producing a temporary disturbance of brain function
Loss of consciousness is not required, and most concussions do not involve it
Symptoms are headache, confusion, feeling dazed or slowed, dizziness, nausea, visual disturbance, and sensitivity to light and noise
Amnesia around the event is common: being unable to recall the moments before or after is a significant finding
Repeating the same question, or seeming vague and slowed, is often the first thing bystanders notice
Symptoms can appear or worsen over hours, so a patient who seems fine now is not cleared
Anyone with a suspected concussion stops the activity and does not return to it the same day
A second head injury before the first has recovered can be far more serious than either would have been
Red flags requiring urgent assessment include worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, increasing drowsiness, weakness or a deteriorating level of consciousness
misconceptions: Believing a concussion requires loss of consciousness
Allowing a player back into a game after a head injury
Treating a well-seeming patient as cleared
Dismissing repeated questioning as ordinary shock
exam_favorites: Loss of consciousness is not required
No return to activity the same day
Red flags that need urgent assessment

read.plain:
A concussion is a brain injury. The word sounds mild and the injury is not — it is a disturbance of brain function caused by force transmitted to the head, whether the head was struck directly or the force arrived through the body.

Start by correcting the belief that gets in the way of everything else: you do not have to be knocked out to have a concussion. Most concussions do not involve any loss of consciousness at all. 'He never went out' is not a reason to relax, and it is offered constantly, usually by somebody who wants the game to continue.

What you see: headache. Confusion. A patient who seems dazed, slowed, foggy, 'not quite there'. Dizziness. Nausea. Blurred or double vision. Sensitivity to light and noise. They may be unusually emotional or irritable in a way that is out of character.

Amnesia around the event is important. Not remembering the moments before the impact, or the moments after, is a significant finding, and it is worth asking about specifically: what is the last thing you remember before? What is the first thing after?

And the thing bystanders notice first — before any of the medical signs — is repetition. Asking the same question two or three times. 'What happened?' answered, and asked again a minute later. That is a brain not laying down new memory properly, and a teammate or a parent will often report it before you have asked anything.

Symptoms evolve. Someone can seem entirely fine on scene and develop a significant headache, nausea and confusion over the following hours. So nobody is cleared by looking well at the roadside. Say that plainly to the patient and to whoever is with them, and make sure somebody will be with them.

On returning to activity, the position is simple and not negotiable: if concussion is suspected, the activity stops and they do not go back to it that day. No exceptions for how important the match is or how much they insist they are fine.

The reason is the second impact. A brain that has been concussed and has not recovered is vulnerable, and a second head injury during that window can produce swelling far out of proportion to the force involved. It is rare and it is catastrophic, and it is entirely preventable by not letting somebody back on.

Red flags mean urgent assessment now rather than watchful waiting: a headache that keeps worsening, repeated vomiting, a seizure, increasing drowsiness or difficulty waking, weakness or numbness, slurred speech, unequal pupils, or any fall in level of consciousness. Those move the patient from concussion to a possible bleed.
read.standard: Concussion denotes traumatic brain injury producing transient disturbance of cerebral function following force transmitted to the head, whether by direct impact or transmitted through the body. Loss of consciousness is not required and is absent in most cases. Clinical features comprise headache, confusion, feeling dazed or cognitively slowed, dizziness, nausea, visual disturbance, photophobia, phonophobia and uncharacteristic emotional lability. Peri-event amnesia, retrograde or anterograde, constitutes a significant finding elicited by specific questioning. Repetitive questioning reflects impaired memory consolidation and is frequently the earliest observation reported by bystanders. Symptoms may develop or progress over hours, so apparent wellness at initial assessment does not constitute clearance. Suspected concussion mandates cessation of activity with no same-day return. Repeat head injury prior to recovery may produce cerebral oedema disproportionate to the force involved, a rare and catastrophic outcome preventable by removal from activity. Red flags requiring urgent evaluation comprise progressive headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, increasing somnolence, focal weakness, dysarthria, pupillary inequality and any decline in level of consciousness.

eli_new.analogy: The brain is a processor that has been dropped. It still runs, it just runs slower and loses things it was told a minute ago.
eli_new.body: Two sentences to have ready, because you will need them. 'You do not have to be knocked out to have a concussion.' And 'He is not going back on today.' Both will be argued with, and neither is negotiable.

concepts.title: Eye, ear, nose and dental injuries
key_points: Do not remove an impaled object from an eye — stabilise it and cover both eyes to stop tracking movement
Cover both eyes for any serious eye injury, because the eyes move together and movement of the good eye moves the injured one
Explain what you are doing before covering both eyes, because sudden blindness is frightening
For chemical in the eye, irrigate immediately and copiously from the inner corner outwards, and keep going per protocol
Irrigate away from the uninjured eye so you do not wash chemical into it
Do not attempt to replace a displaced eyeball; cover it with a moist sterile dressing and a protective shield
Do not remove contact lenses unless there is a chemical burn and your protocol directs it
For a knocked-out tooth, handle it by the crown and not the root, keep it moist, and bring it — milk or the patient's own saliva per protocol
For ear injuries, do not pack the canal, particularly where cerebrospinal fluid may be draining
misconceptions: Removing an impaled object from an eye
Covering only the injured eye
Handling an avulsed tooth by its root
Letting an avulsed tooth dry out

exam_favorites: Irrigate inner to outer, away from the good eye

read.plain:
The eyes move together. That single fact drives most of eye injury care.

When the good eye looks left, the injured eye looks left too, whether it should or not. So for any serious eye injury — and especially an impaled object or a penetrating injury — you cover both eyes. Covering only the injured one leaves it tracking every movement of the other, which drags on the wound.

That is uncomfortable to do, because covering both eyes makes someone suddenly blind, in pain, in a strange environment, in the back of an ambulance. So explain first, explain properly, and keep talking to them. Tell them what you are doing and why, tell them who is with them, describe what is happening around them. A frightened patient who cannot see needs your voice more than anything else you can offer.

An impaled object in an eye is never removed. Stabilise it — a cup or cone over it, secured without pressing on it — and cover both eyes.

Chemical in the eye is the one true eye emergency where you make a large difference. Irrigate immediately, copiously, and for far longer than feels necessary, per protocol. Direction matters: irrigate from the inner corner outwards, so the fluid runs away from the nose rather than across it. If you irrigate the wrong way you wash the chemical straight into the other eye, and a patient with one injured eye becomes a patient with two. Contact lenses come out for a chemical burn if protocol directs it; otherwise leave them alone.

If an eyeball has been displaced from its socket, do not try to push it back. Cover it with a moist sterile dressing, protect it with a shield that does not press on it, cover the other eye, and go.

Teeth. A tooth that has been knocked out can often be reimplanted, and how it is handled decides whether that works. Hold it by the crown — the part you chew with — never by the root. The root surface carries the cells that allow reattachment, and handling or scrubbing them destroys it. Do not scrub it clean. Keep it moist: milk is commonly recommended, and the patient's own saliva works, per your protocol. Never let it dry out, and bring it with the patient. Also check that a missing tooth is not in the airway.

Ears: do not pack the canal. That applies particularly where clear fluid may be draining after head trauma, where packing risks raising pressure and driving contamination inward. Cover loosely and let it drain.
read.standard: Conjugate eye movement dictates management: bilateral occlusion is required for significant unilateral injury, as movement of the uninjured eye produces corresponding movement of the injured one. Patients require explanation and continued verbal contact, as sudden bilateral occlusion produces significant distress. Impaled ocular objects are stabilised without pressure and not removed. Chemical exposure requires immediate copious irrigation from the medial to lateral canthus, directing fluid away from the contralateral eye to prevent cross-contamination, continued per protocol; contact lens removal is indicated in chemical injury where protocol directs. Globe avulsion is managed by moist sterile covering and a protective shield without replacement attempt. Avulsed teeth may be reimplanted; handling is confined to the crown, as root surface cells permitting reattachment are destroyed by handling or cleaning. The tooth is kept moist in milk or the patient's saliva per protocol, never permitted to desiccate, and transported with the patient; airway assessment for missing dentition is required. Aural canal packing is contraindicated, particularly where cerebrospinal fluid leak is suspected.

eli_new.body: Irrigate from the nose outwards, never across. Get that direction wrong on a chemical splash and you have taken a patient with one damaged eye and given them two.

concepts.title: Neck injuries and open neck wounds
key_points: The neck contains the airway, the major vessels to and from the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves, all in a small space with little protection
An open neck wound involving a large vein can draw air into the circulation, which can be rapidly fatal
Cover an open neck wound with an occlusive dressing to keep air out, and apply direct pressure to control bleeding
Never apply circumferential pressure or a dressing all the way around the neck
Press on the wound, not around the neck, and hold it manually rather than relying on a bandage
Expanding swelling or a growing haematoma in the neck can compress the airway, so the airway is watched continuously
Hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, air bubbling from a wound, or crackling under the skin suggest injury to the airway itself
Assume spinal injury with any significant neck trauma, and maintain manual in-line stabilisation while managing everything else
These patients deteriorate quickly, so transport early with a pre-alert
misconceptions: Bandaging circumferentially around the neck
Leaving an open neck wound uncovered
Relying on a bandage rather than a hand for pressure
Not watching the airway while managing the bleeding

read.plain:
Everything important passes through the neck, in a small space, with very little protecting it. The airway. The arteries carrying blood to the brain. The large veins carrying it back. The spinal cord. Major nerves. A wound in that space can involve several of those at once.

One danger is particular to the neck and worth understanding rather than memorising. The large veins there operate at low pressure, and when the chest expands during a breath, pressure inside them can fall below atmospheric. An open wound into such a vein can therefore draw air in — and air entering the circulation in volume can be rapidly fatal.

That is why an open neck wound gets an occlusive dressing. Not just any dressing — one that does not let air through. It serves two purposes at once: keeping air out, and holding pressure on the bleeding.

Control the bleeding with direct pressure on the wound. And now the rule that matters most, because breaking it can kill somebody: never apply pressure all the way around the neck. Do not wrap a bandage around it. Do not tie anything around it. The patient has an airway and a second carotid artery in there, and circumferential pressure compromises both.

So: press on the wound with your hand, and keep your hand there. Manual pressure is better here than any securing method, because you can direct it precisely at the wound and nowhere else. If you must secure it, the standard approach is to bandage over the dressing and under the opposite armpit — which holds it firmly without going around the neck.

The second danger is swelling. A haematoma in the neck expands into a space with nowhere to go, and the thing it compresses is the airway. A patient talking normally now can have a rapidly enlarging swelling that closes their airway over minutes. So you watch the airway continuously, not once. Listen to the voice.

Signs that the airway itself is injured: hoarseness or a changed voice, difficulty swallowing, air bubbling out of the wound with breathing, and crackling under the skin when you touch it, which is air in the tissues. Any of those means the airway has been breached, and it is a reason to be moving.

Assume a spinal injury with any significant neck trauma and maintain manual in-line stabilisation throughout — but not at the cost of the airway or the bleeding, which come first.

These patients can go from talking to critical in a short time. Transport early and pre-alert.
read.standard: The cervical region contains the airway, carotid and vertebral arteries, jugular venous system, spinal cord and major nerves within a confined, poorly protected space. Open wounds involving large cervical veins risk venous air embolism, as negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration may entrain air, potentially producing rapid fatality. Occlusive dressing is therefore indicated, providing both air exclusion and haemorrhage control. Circumferential pressure or bandaging is absolutely contraindicated owing to airway and contralateral carotid compromise; manual direct pressure over the wound is preferred, with securing achieved by bandaging over the dressing and beneath the contralateral axilla. Expanding cervical haematoma compresses the airway within a non-expansile space, potentially producing obstruction over minutes in an initially conversational patient, requiring continuous airway monitoring including voice assessment. Findings suggesting laryngotracheal injury comprise hoarseness or voice change, dysphagia, air bubbling from the wound and subcutaneous emphysema. Spinal injury is assumed with significant cervical trauma, with manual in-line stabilisation maintained, subordinate to airway and haemorrhage priorities. Early transport with prearrival notification is indicated.

eli_new.analogy: The neck is a corridor with everything running through it and no walls. A wound there is never just one injury.
eli_new.body: Never wrap anything around a neck. Your hand goes on the wound and stays there, and if it has to be secured, it goes over the dressing and under the opposite armpit.

read.plain:
Spinal care has changed substantially, and it is worth understanding why rather than just learning the new rules.

For decades, anybody with a mechanism that could conceivably have injured a spine was strapped to a long rigid board with a collar and blocks. It felt careful and responsible.

Then the harms were examined properly. Rigid boards cause pressure injuries quickly — measurably, within under an hour. They are extremely uncomfortable, which causes patients to move more, not less. They restrict chest expansion and make breathing harder. They make airway management difficult, and a patient who vomits while strapped supine to a board is a serious problem. And the evidence that they prevented spinal cord injury turned out to be thin.

Meanwhile, a genuinely unstable spinal injury is uncommon, and most patients being boarded had no spinal injury at all.

So practice moved to selective spinal motion restriction: deciding based on the patient rather than the mechanism.

The criteria usually consider: is the patient alert and oriented, or is their mental status altered? Are they intoxicated? Is there any neurological deficit — weakness, numbness, tingling? Is there midline tenderness when you palpate the spine itself, as opposed to the muscles beside it? And is there a distracting injury — something painful enough that they might not notice a sore back?

A patient who is alert, sober, neurologically intact, without midline tenderness and without a distracting injury generally does not need restriction, however dramatic their crash was.

The specific criteria are set by your service, and they differ between systems. Use yours, from the protocol, not a half-remembered version from a textbook or another state.

When restriction is indicated, the goal has shifted too. It is to minimise movement, not to achieve rigid immobilisation — which was never really achievable anyway. In practice that usually means a correctly sized cervical collar, the patient moved with a scoop stretcher rather than log rolled, placed on a padded ambulance stretcher, handled as little as possible, and transported smoothly.

The long backboard still exists and still has a job: getting someone out of a vehicle or a difficult space. It is an extrication device. They come off it once they are on the stretcher.

And underneath all of this, manual in-line stabilisation remains the foundation. Somebody's hands holding the head in a neutral position, applied early and maintained while everything else happens. It is free, it causes no harm, and it is the most effective spinal precaution you have.
read.standard: Contemporary practice employs selective spinal motion restriction in place of universal immobilisation based on mechanism. This change reflects documented harms of long spine boards — pressure injury developing within under an hour, pain producing increased patient movement, restricted chest expansion, and impaired airway management, particularly with emesis in supine restrained patients — alongside limited evidence of benefit, and the low prevalence of unstable spinal injury among immobilised patients. Selective criteria typically assess mental status, intoxication, neurological deficit, midline spinal tenderness as distinct from paraspinal tenderness, and the presence of distracting injury. Patients who are alert, unintoxicated, neurologically intact, without midline tenderness and without distracting injury generally do not require restriction. Criteria are established locally and vary between systems. Where restriction is indicated, the objective is minimisation of movement rather than rigid immobilisation: appropriately sized cervical collar, scoop stretcher transfer in preference to log rolling, padded stretcher, minimal handling and smooth transport. The long spine board functions as an extrication device, with removal following transfer. Manual in-line stabilisation constitutes the foundation of spinal precaution, applied early and maintained throughout.

eli_new.analogy: The board was a device for reassuring the crew. It was not evidence, and the patients on it were paying for that reassurance in pressure injuries.
eli_new.body: Two hands on a head, held neutral, costs nothing and harms nobody, and it is the most effective spinal precaution you have. Everything after that is a decision about devices; this bit is just doing it.

concepts.title: Neurogenic shock
key_points: Neurogenic shock follows a spinal cord injury that interrupts the nerves controlling blood vessel tone
The vessels dilate and the container becomes too large for the volume inside it, so the pressure falls
Nothing has been lost — this is a distribution problem, not a volume problem, which is why it looks different from bleeding
The skin is warm, dry and often flushed below the level of injury, rather than cool and clammy
The pulse is normal or slow rather than fast, because the nerves that would speed the heart have also been interrupted
A hypotensive trauma patient with a slow pulse and warm dry skin is the classic picture
Never assume neurogenic shock until haemorrhage has been excluded, because a bleeding patient can also have a spinal injury
These patients lose the ability to regulate their temperature and become hypothermic quickly
Spinal shock is a different thing: a temporary loss of cord function below the injury, not a circulatory problem

exam_favorites: Why the skin is warm and the pulse slow
A distribution problem, not a volume problem

read.plain:
Neurogenic shock is the one type of shock that looks nothing like the others, and understanding why makes it easy to remember.

The nerves that keep blood vessels partly constricted run down the spinal cord and out to the body. A cord injury can interrupt them. When that happens, everything below the injury relaxes and dilates.

Now think about the plumbing. The volume of blood has not changed at all — none has been lost. But the container holding it has suddenly become much larger. The same amount of fluid in a larger space means lower pressure everywhere.

This is a distribution problem, not a volume problem. And that single distinction explains every finding.

Why is the skin warm, dry and often flushed? Because in haemorrhagic shock the body clamps down the skin vessels to push blood to the core, which gives you the classic pale, cool, clammy patient. Here, the nerves that would do that clamping have been cut. The vessels stay open. The skin stays warm and pink and dry.

Why is the pulse normal or slow rather than fast? Same reason. Bleeding makes the heart speed up because the nervous system drives it to. Those same nerves have been interrupted, so the heart does not respond. In some cord injuries the unopposed slowing influence makes the pulse frankly slow.

So the picture to memorise is: a hypotensive trauma patient with a slow pulse and warm, dry, flushed skin. Everything is the opposite of what shock is supposed to look like, and that is why it is recognisable.

Now the safety rule, which matters more than the recognition. Never assume neurogenic shock until you have excluded bleeding. A patient with a spinal cord injury has been in something violent, and that same violence breaks spleens and pelvises and femurs. If you decide early that low pressure is neurogenic, you stop looking for the bleeding, and the bleeding is the thing that kills them. Neurogenic shock is what you conclude after searching, not what you assume instead of searching.

Temperature deserves attention. These patients cannot regulate their own temperature below the injury — they cannot shiver, cannot constrict skin vessels — so they take on the temperature of their surroundings. They get cold fast, and cold makes bleeding worse and everything else harder. Blankets, early, and keep the compartment warm.

One piece of vocabulary to keep straight. Spinal shock is not the same thing and is not a circulatory problem at all. It is a temporary loss of cord function below the injury — flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes — which may recover partly or wholly over time. Neurogenic shock is about blood pressure. Spinal shock is about cord function. The words are similar and they mean different things.
read.standard: Neurogenic shock results from spinal cord injury interrupting sympathetic vasomotor innervation, producing vasodilation below the level of injury. Circulating volume is unchanged; increased vascular capacitance relative to fixed volume produces hypotension, constituting distributive rather than hypovolaemic shock. Cutaneous findings are warm, dry and frequently flushed skin below the injury, reflecting absent compensatory vasoconstriction. Heart rate is normal or bradycardic, as sympathetic chronotropic drive is interrupted with unopposed vagal influence. The characteristic presentation comprises hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin in a trauma patient. Haemorrhage must be excluded before attributing hypotension to neurogenic causes, as the mechanisms producing cord injury also produce intra-abdominal, pelvic and long bone haemorrhage; premature attribution terminates the search for the treatable cause. Thermoregulation is impaired below the injury, with absent shivering and cutaneous vasoconstriction producing rapid poikilothermic heat loss; active warming is indicated. Spinal shock is a distinct entity denoting transient loss of cord function below the injury with flaccid paralysis and areflexia, potentially recovering over time, and is not a circulatory phenomenon.

eli_new.analogy: The blood did not leave. The container got bigger. Same water, wider tank, lower level everywhere.
eli_new.body: Neurogenic shock is a conclusion, never an assumption. The moment you decide low pressure is neurogenic, you stop looking for the bleed — and that patient was in something violent enough to break a spine, which is violent enough to break a spleen.

His pressure was 78 systolic, his pulse was 56, and his skin was warm, dry and pink.

He had fallen far enough to break his spine, which is far enough to break a spleen. Neurogenic shock is what you conclude after looking, not instead of looking.

concepts.title: Helmet removal
key_points: A helmet is left in place if the airway is clear, it fits snugly, and the head can be immobilised within it
It is removed if it interferes with the airway or ventilation, if it is loose enough that the head moves inside it, or if it prevents immobilisation
It is also removed for cardiac arrest, where chest compressions and full airway access are needed
Removal is always a two-person procedure — one maintains stabilisation while the other removes
The person maintaining stabilisation changes hands part way through, taking hold from below so the head is never unsupported
Full-face helmets need the visor removed and the sides spread to clear the nose and ears
Motorcycle helmets and sports helmets differ; some sports helmets are designed for the facemask to be removed while leaving the helmet on
Remove shoulder pads and helmet together where both are worn, because removing one alone changes the head position
Move slowly and stop if there is resistance, pain, or any change in neurological findings
misconceptions: Removing a helmet single-handed
Removing a helmet that is doing no harm
Removing a sports helmet when only the facemask needed to come off
Removing a helmet and leaving shoulder pads on
exam_favorites: When to leave a helmet on

read.plain:
The starting position is that helmets usually stay on. A well-fitting helmet holds the head securely, and taking it off requires moving that head.

Leave it on if three things are true: the airway is clear and you can manage the breathing, it fits snugly with no movement of the head inside, and you can immobilise the head adequately with it in place.

Take it off if any of those fail. If you cannot access or manage the airway. If it is loose enough that the head moves independently inside it — in which case it is providing no stabilisation and is actively in the way. If it prevents you immobilising the head properly. And in cardiac arrest, where you need full airway access and the patient flat for compressions.

The principle is simple: a helmet that is helping stays; a helmet that is preventing something necessary comes off.

Removal is a two-person job and cannot safely be done alone. That is not a preference.

Person one takes the head first, usually reaching in from the sides at the base of the helmet and supporting the mandible and the occiput. Person two then works the helmet.

The important part is the handover in the middle. Person two spreads the sides of the helmet and eases it off, and at a certain point person one has to change their hold — taking the head from below, hands under the occiput and supporting the jaw, so the head stays supported while the helmet passes over it. That transfer, done slowly and with both people talking, is the whole skill. Done badly, the head drops backwards when the helmet clears it, because the helmet had been holding it.

Practical details. Full-face helmets need the visor taken off first, and the sides spread outwards to clear the nose — a full-face helmet will not come off a face without that. Glasses come off first.

Sports helmets are different from motorcycle helmets. Many are designed so that the facemask comes off while the helmet stays on, which gives you full airway access without moving the head at all. Where that is possible it is much better than removal.

And where shoulder pads are worn with a helmet — American football, some other sports — they are a matched pair. Removing the helmet alone leaves the pads propping the shoulders up and the head falls back into extension; removing the pads alone does the reverse. Take both, or neither.

Throughout: slowly. If you meet resistance, or the patient reports pain, or anything changes neurologically, stop and reassess. There is no version of this that should be done quickly.
read.standard: Helmets are retained where the airway is accessible and manageable, the fit is snug without independent head movement, and adequate immobilisation is achievable in situ. Removal is indicated where the helmet impedes airway access or ventilation, where fit permits independent head movement, where it precludes adequate immobilisation, and in cardiac arrest requiring full airway access and supine positioning. Removal is a two-person procedure. The first provider establishes stabilisation from the sides, supporting mandible and occiput. The second provider removes the visor, spreads the helmet laterally to clear the nose and auricles, and eases it off. Mid-procedure the first provider transfers hold to an inferior approach, supporting occiput and mandible from below, maintaining continuous support as the helmet passes; failure of this transfer permits occipital drop as the supporting helmet clears. Sports helmets frequently permit facemask removal with helmet retention, providing airway access without head movement, which is preferred where available. Where shoulder pads accompany a helmet, both are removed together, as isolated removal of either alters head position into extension or flexion. The procedure is performed slowly, with cessation for resistance, pain or neurological change.

eli_new.analogy: The helmet has been holding the head. The moment it clears, whatever your hands are not doing, gravity is.
eli_new.body: The whole skill is the handover in the middle. One set of hands has to take the head from below before the helmet passes over it, and if that transfer is rushed the head drops the moment the helmet clears.

story.title: The head dropped
story.dispatch: Training debrief — helmet removal, practical assessment.
story.body:
The removal went well right up to the last moment, when the helmet cleared and the head dropped back two or three centimetres onto the mat.

The student holding stabilisation had not changed their hold and had nothing underneath the occiput.

The helmet had been doing that job for them the entire time, and it stopped the instant it came off.
